slides.sub: Here's the truth about title insurance: there can be 2 at closing, and only 1 protects you.

slides.label: Step 1:
slides.title: The lender's policy protects the lender
slides.body: It's usually required to get a mortgage, and it only covers claims that affect the loan.
slides.source: CFPB, What is lender's title insurance? (Oct. 2026)

slides.label: Step 2:
slides.title: It doesn't protect your equity
slides.body: If someone sues with a claim against your home, you're the first person responsible.
slides.source: CFPB, What is lender's title insurance? (Oct. 2026)

slides.label: Step 3:
slides.title: Ask about an owner's policy
slides.body: To protect your equity if a title problem comes up, the CFPB says you may want one. Talk to a real estate attorney about your situation.
slides.source: CFPB, What is lender's title insurance? (Oct. 2026)

slides.label: Step 4:
slides.title: The seller can't force a title company on you
slides.body: With a federally related mortgage, the seller can't require a particular title company.

caption:
Here's the truth about title insurance: there can be 2 policies at closing, and only 1 of them covers you.

The lender's title policy is usually required to get a mortgage. It protects your lender and only covers claims that affect the loan. It doesn't protect your equity.

To protect your equity if a title problem comes up, ask about an owner's title policy.

One more: if you're buying with a federally related mortgage, federal law (RESPA) says the seller can't require you to buy title insurance from a particular company.

Talk to a real estate attorney about your situation.
